newsitem.title: USA: Early U.S. soy harvest may not avert supply crunch.
newsitem.headline: Early U.S. soy harvest may not avert supply crunch.

text.p: The expected jump in southern U.S. soybean acreage will increase the number of early bushels harvested, but early supplies might not be large enough to ease an expected supply crunch in August and September, crop observers said.

"We'll see some August soybeans (in Louisiana), but only a very limited supply in the southeast from the sugar cane growing areas," said David Bollich, grain marking specialist for the Louisana Farm Bureau in Baton Rouge.
"But we'll have more early bushels than we normally do because more early maturing varieties were planted," he said.
In Louisana, the U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast the number of harvested acres to climb to 1.35 million acres during 1997/98 (Aug/Sep) from 1.08 million a year ago.
Farmers in the South, enticed by the spring's 8-1/2-year highs in soybean prices, planted more soybean acres.

More early maturing varieties were also planted in an attempt to capture the premium that prices in August and September hold to November when the bulk of the U.S. Midwest crop is harvested, crop specialists said.

But the bulk of those crops will not be available in time to ease the tight supplies seen for August and early September, when U.S. and South American old crop supplies are nearly exhausted, crop sources said.
In its latest supply and demand forecast in June, USDA projected U.S. soybean ending stocks will be hovering near 20-year lows at 130 million bushels when the marketing year ends August 31.
Additionally, Brazilian farmers are said to have committed 84 percent of their 1996/97 (Feb/Jan) crop and some firms have already purchased U.S. soybeans for fall delivery to meet export commitments.
"I'm really worried about what will be available in September," said one Indiana soybean crusher. "We'll see some crushable volumes of beans the last week in September, but just a few."
In Mississippi, where USDA has forecast a 17 percent increase in harvested soybean acres, the bulk of the soybean crop is not expected to be harvested until mid-September to late October.

"We could see early beans in the middle of August, but from September 10 to October 20 is when we see the most active harvesting," said Thomas Gregory with the Mississippi Agricultural Statistics Service. The Mississippi harvest could also run a few weeks late this year because wet weather delayed soybean plantings, Gregory said.

The soybean crop in Arkansas will also be postponed somewhat by ongoing wet and cool weather in that state, but some early maturing soybean varieties could be ready for harvest by the end of August, said Lanny Ashlock, soybean agronomist with the University of Arkansas in Little Rock.
"We'll have a little September production because we're planting more early maturing varieties," Ashlock said.
USDA has estimated 1997/98 harvested acreage in Arkansas at 3.55 million acres, up from last year's 3.50 million.

In North Carolina, where USDA has projected farmers will harvest 1.28 million acres of soybeans, an official with the N.C. Department of Agriculture said that active harvest would not be seen until late October.
"We could see some early beans in October, but generally farmers here harvest all the other crops first," said Nick Lassiter, the agency's grain marketing specialist.
